articles.title_orig: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’
articles.title_zh: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’
articles.content_orig:
Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton over John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for Republicans
US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized Donald Trump , his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary.
“He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary.
“John Cornyn’s a great member of the US Senate. Paxton has his challenges,” the retiring Tillis added. “We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in Texas if Cornyn had won.”
Tillis pointed to the president’s involvement in the contest and described Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of Cornyn as an “unforced error” that has put the Senate seat at risk for the GOP.
Trump endorsed Paxton just days before the Texas attorney general defeated Cornyn, a four-term senator, and advanced to face Democratic candidate James Talarico, a in the general election on 3 November.
The race had wide implications for Trump’s strength heading into November’s midterm federal elections. Paxton will now face Talarico, a Democratic pastor and state legislator whose message of peace and populism has attracted much attention. If he wins, Talarico would become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide office in Texas.
When he chose to support Paxton over Cornyn, Trump highlighted the Texas attorney general’s record as a steadfast supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
Cornyn had previously said during the 2024 presidential campaign that Republicans should move on from Trump.
In a social media post shortly before the election day, Trump said Cornyn had been “VERY disloyal” to him and implored voters in Texas to “REMEMBER!”
Paxton, meanwhile, is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud, but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement.
In July 2025, his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “ on biblical grounds ”, citing adultery.
Tillis is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions. In April, he spoke out in defense of the Nato military alliance after Trump said he was “absolutely” considering withdrawing the US from it.
“Any president that contemplates attempting to withdraw from Nato is not only fulfilling [Russian leader] Vladimir Putin and [Chinese premier] Xi Jinping’s greatest dreams but would be undermining America’s own national security interests,” Tillis said at the time.
He also called for then secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem’s resignation after immigration agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis in January, calling her leadership “ a disaster ” during the last Senate hearing before her firing.
Tillis was one of a small number of Republicans on Thursday to vote in favor of a Democrat-led war powers resolution that aimed to end the US war with Iran. Despite gaining some Republican support, the proposal failed to pass in the Senate by a 49-50 vote.

articles.title_orig: China weighs allowing ByteDance, Alibaba to buy new Nvidia chips, The Information reports
articles.title_zh: China weighs allowing ByteDance, Alibaba to buy new Nvidia chips, The Information reports
articles.content_orig:
The Chinese government has signaled it could allow some domestic companies like ByteDance and Alibaba to buy Nvidia's chip built for high-end professional computers, The Information reported on Sunday, citing two people familiar with the matter.
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology recently asked companies including ByteDance and Alibaba to report their plans to purchase Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 chips, according to the report.
The ministry told some Chinese companies the government intends to approve the purchases, The Information report said, adding that some industry executives expect the RTX PRO 5500 chip to avoid U.S. export restrictions.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
"US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly half a decade ago, and China's own limits on US imports," an Nvidia spokesperson said when asked to comment.
Alibaba and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately reach the Chinese government for comment.

articles.title_orig: Rihanna Celebrates Daughter Rocki's First Birthday With Never-Before-Seen Photos and Videos
articles.title_zh: Rihanna Celebrates Daughter Rocki's First Birthday With Never-Before-Seen Photos and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Rihanna and A$AP Rocky 's daughter Rocki is shining bright on her big day.
The “Diamonds” singer shared rare photos of her and the “Sundress” hitmaker’s little girl in honor of the toddler’s first birthday—and it’s safe to say she’s her mother’s daughter.
In the first clip shared to Rihanna’s Instagram Sept. 26, it seems Rocki got her name from being able to rock any look. After all, the toddler was filmed in her highchair as she sported one of her mom’s wigs.
As Rihanna said in the clip through laughs, “Wow, baby.”
Another adorable snap sealed the deal that the 12-month-old is following in her mom’s beauty-loving footsteps as she was seen wearing pink hair curlers. Meanwhile, separate footage showed a glammed up Rocki playing with a product from her mom’s Fenty beauty line.
Plus, the tot showed off her passion for fashion as she played with her mom’s Louis Vuitton bag in separate video. And after the Grammy winner took the bag from her daughter—who was dressed in a tan onesie—she had four five seconds to hand the goods back over as Rocki began to cry, only to be soothed after the designer duds were back in her possession.
Other adorable moments in the carousel included a video of a newborn Rocki cuddling up to her mom, a clip of Rihanna trying to get her baby girl to say “mama,” and a snap of the toddler lounging in a bikini.
And the “Umbrella” singer knows her youngest child is a whole vibe. As she captioned the post, “Who let me have a daughter, bro?”
Recently, Rihanna—also mom to sons RZA , 4, and Riot , 3, with A$AP Rocky—shared another set of rare family photos, this time in her native Barbados.
"One minute I feel like that kid from Westbury," the 38-year-old captioned the photo featuring her three little ones posing in front of her childhood home, shared to Instagram Aug. 11. "The next minute I’m bringing my own kids back to 'Rihanna Drive.'"
The cultural landmark, established in 2017, allows fans to visit the colorful building that Rihanna (born Robyn Rihanna Fenty ) grew up in within the suburbs of Bridgetown.
"Trippy how life works!" the Anti artist continued. "And the Glory STILL and WILL ALWAYS belong to the Almighty Creator!!!"
Since welcoming her three kids, Rihanna has been candid about how motherhood has changed her.
“I’m actually afraid of s--t,” she told Interview Magazine in 2024. “The well-being of your kids, you worry about that constantly. Nobody warns you that having kids means you’re going to worry every second of your life.”
But it’s all worth it if it means being RZA, Riot and Rocki’s mom.
"They bring purpose to every aspect of my life," she told E! News that same year. "Everything has to be intentional, and everything has to be worth it—especially when it takes me away from them."
Keep reading for a look back at Rihanna and A$AP Rocky's road to parenthood…
In 2012, Rihanna and A$AP Rocky performed their hit "Cockiness" at the MTV Video Music Awards, and their number was so good it deserved a trophy. This wouldn't be the last time the two shared the stage as they went on tour together in 2013.
Fans had this song on replay after Rihanna and A$AP Rocky released the music video for "Fashion Killa" in 2013.
As the years went on, they remained friends. In 2018, they attended the Louis Vuitton Menswear Spring/Summer 2019 show as part of Paris Fashion Week and, of course, they totally slayed.
They also attended The Fashion Awards in 2019, with Rihanna dazzling in a mint Fenty dress and A$AP Rocky looking sharp in a black suit.
Met Gala official! Rihanna and A$AP Rocky attended the 2021 Met Gala together in style, with the "Umbrella" singer wearing a black Balenciaga gown and the "A$AP Forever" artist donning a custom ERL quilt and a tuxedo.
After announcing they were expecting their first baby, Rihanna recalled keeping her pregnancy a secret from her friends . "It was harder for me to keep it from my posse, because they're around me, they know my habits," she told E!'s Justin Sylvester . "They're like, 'You don't want something to drink? You're not smoking?' And I'm eating all the things I'm not used to eating. They know I hate sweets and I'm all of a sudden asking for cookies and donuts. But finally, I just had to let it all out, and they were all shocked, of course, as the world was shocked as well."
SOS! These photos are so sweet! As Rihanna and A$AP prepared for their bundle of joy, she continued to show her incredible pregnancy style.
While fans wondered if A$AP Rocky had proposed to Rihanna after seeing them sport the words "Marry me?" and "I do" across their teeth in his "D.M.B." video, sources close to the couple told TMZ in May 2022 the two aren't engaged.
And baby makes three! Multiple outlets report that the couple welcomed a baby in Los Angeles.
She debuted her second pregnancy during the 2023 Super Bowl halftime show.
The pair take the 2023 Met Gala together in honor of Chanel designer Karl Lagerfeld.
Rihanna accompanied A$AP Rocky during his performance at a Spotify party in Cannes, France.
The couple welcomed their second child, son Riot . One month later, they shared their first photos as a family of four in a rare photoshoot.
Rihanna confirmed her romance with A$AP began at the end of 2019 .
"I've seen him in relationships. He's seen me in relationships," she explained in a conversation for Interview published April 9 . "We knew what we're capable of, and the trouble that we could bring to each other's lives. We can make or break each other's hearts. And so, we started dating with a lot of caution."
Baby No. 3! Shortly before arriving to the 2025 Met Gala, the "Love on the Brain" singer confirmed her pregnancy .
Rihanna announced the birth of her daughter Rocki Irish Mayers with a pair of Instagram photos of herself holding the newborn as a set of pink boxing gloves.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s latest Mamdani lovefest comes at a bad time for Republicans
articles.title_zh: Trump’s latest Mamdani lovefest comes at a bad time for Republicans
articles.content_orig:
President Trump invited lefty Mayor Zohran Mamdani to visit him at the White House to “see how I work” after a meeting at Gracie Mansion Monday , a lip reader revealed.
“What I will say, we’ll look after you, but as I say, you’re doing great ,” Trump said, expert lip reader Jeremy Freeman told The Post.
“I’ll look after you, you look after the New Yorkers,” the president said. “And we can both make it work. I wanna support you, help me. Come with me to the White House – see how I work.”
The 90-minute meeting focused on immigration and a Queens housing project for which Mamdani is seeking federal help, with Trump also sharing memories of Gracie Mansion.
It was the first presidential visit to the mayor’s official residence since Ronald Reagan visited Ed Koch in 1981 to tout federal investments in a local roadway project.
The Sunnyside Yards affordable housing project was revived by Mamdani earlier this year after lying dormant for decades — but it needs an infusion of federal dollars to help get it done.
“We appreciate the president’s commitment to the city,” Mamdani told reporters at a briefing after the meeting. “And today, you know, the president shared many of his memories of having been to Gracie Mansion before, having been out here, as well on the lawn. And we appreciated the conversation of how we can work together to deliver a lower cost of living for New Yorkers.”
The socialist mayor and the president, a conservative Republican, struck up an unusual friendship after a White House meeting in February , with Trump telling reporters, “I think he’s a nice guy.”
Mamdani later called the encounter “a productive meeting.”
“I’m looking forward to building more housing in New York City,” the mayor said after the February Oval Office meeting in a post on X, that also included a doctored pic showing Trump holding two copies of the New York Daily News.
One shows the real 1975 headline, “Ford to City: Drop Dead,” and the other a mocked-up version: ‘Trump to City: Let’s Build.”
The chummy chat was at odds with an initial exchange of barbs that saw Mamdani refer to Trump as a “fascist” and a “despot,” while the president referred to the mayor as a communist.
But following Monday’s Big Apple reunion, Trump again had kind words for Mamdani.
“I’ve seen it with numerous different mayors, and I said some great ones and some not so great ones,” he told Mamdani in front of reporters.
“So, hopefully you’re going to be a great one. I’ll be able to say you’re going to be a great one, and you’re off to a good start.”
Trump’s stopover at Gracie Mansion came with the president’s scheduled speech before the UN General Assembly.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Bill Gates says an AI ‘kill switch’ isn’t enough
articles.title_zh: Bill Gates says an AI ‘kill switch’ isn’t enough
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence ( AI ), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”
Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”
Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.
“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures.
Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.
“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”
Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.
His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.
Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.
Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.
Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday.
The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.
Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.
An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.
Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.
In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”
Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’
“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

OpenAI’s agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics when they couldn’t immediately get what they wanted.
Security researcher Rowan Howard-Jones says that OpenAI agents scanned the UN Conference on Trade and Development’s (UNCTAD) statistics site over 16,000 times between April and June . While the incident doesn’t quite rise to the level of the Hugging Face hack , or the recent attacks on US government sites , it’s yet another concerning example of AI agents going outside the normal bounds to accomplish a task.
According to Howard-Jones, the agents were likely tasked with retrieving publicly available data related to the Productive Capacities Index (PCI) through the UNCTADstat API. However, the agents did not appear to have direct API access and were limited in their ability to pull data from UNCTADstat because of restrictions on their HTTP tools.
The agents eventually worked out a way to bypass their limitations and start pulling data from the site, but still encountered some errors. At this point, the AI went from creative to deceptive. Believing that the errors were due to its requests being caught by a nonexistent filter, it started to mask its behavior. It eventually realized it could hijack Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool) to accomplish its goals. The agents resorted to increasingly aggressive tactics to get access to UN data.
OpenAI and the UN did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

What it’s like to be in Donald Trump’s Cabinet.
In President Donald Trump’s Cabinet, the job description is whatever the president says it is that day, and a secretary’s role can expand or veer with his latest fixation. | Matt Wuerker/POLITICO
President Donald Trump’s mind was on Iran. It was the final weekday of May, and shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz were again unnavigable. Trump had just left the Situation Room and was discussing the issue with several Cabinet officials in the Oval Office when an aide interrupted with some unwelcome news about another waterfront quagmire closer to home.
A federal judge had just ordered Trump’s name removed from the “Trump-Kennedy Center,” as the White House had attempted to relabel the federally administered cultural complex on the Potomac River barely a mile away. While the decision foreclosed the president’s efforts to rebrand the facility, it did leave open a legal path to other objectives in his yearlong quest to remake the storied performing arts institution. Trump could proceed with major renovations, the judge ruled, as long as the center’s board was fully consulted.
As the Kennedy Center drama prepared to shift into a new phase, Trump realized he lacked someone there who could do his bidding. Loyalist Ric Grenell had left the post of executive director two months earlier, replaced by a longtime District of Columbia official who had been the Kennedy’s Center’s vice president of facilities. Trump barely paused to consider his options.
The president looked around the room, and zeroed in on the man who was 10th in the line of presidential succession, whose department had been founded in 1903 with a mandate to “foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce, the mining, manufacturing, shipping, and fishery industries.” It now had nearly 50,000 employees working toward those aims. Not a single one of them had been hired for his or her expertise in performing arts administration. It would now be Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s job, Trump declared, to “fix” the Kennedy Center. One of the country’s oldest government posts had been redefined in an instant.
“If you bring a problem up to the president, and it’s not exactly in your lane, and it’s really not in anybody else’s lane, but there’s a problem, you will inherit that problem,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Because the president will listen to you, get your opinion, and he’ll say, ‘Well, go fix it.’”
Such is life in Trump’s Cabinet, where the job description is whatever the president says it is that day, and a secretary’s role can expand or veer with his latest fixation. (A Commerce Department spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on Lutnick’s Kennedy Center duties.) Unexpected assignments, late-night phone calls seeking their input on matters beyond their official remits and major policy announcements on Truth Social — all can change the course of a secretary’s day, and sometimes a department’s agenda.
If Trump’s first presidency started with an aspiration to be built like a corporation, where headhunters looked for the most impressive résumés to fill top jobs, his second is structured like a family business. A small cast of trusted characters — true believers, there more for their familiarity and loyalty than any objective qualifications — are always at hand, ready to be put on whatever project comes up.
“What you have is a very strong centralized authority figure, and everybody is trying to stay in his good graces and keep him happy from a personality perspective,” said one former senior Trump administration official. “Trump is a very strong monarch, and when you have a strong monarch and weak barons, they’ve got to constantly go to the king for the ability to do anything.”
The story of Trump’s second Cabinet is not, however, just one more installment in a long history of federal departments losing power to the “presidential branch,” as political scientist Matthew Dickinson has described a phenomenon he traces back to Franklin D. Roosevelt. Trump’s top appointees have had more personal exposure to the president than many of their predecessors. But that access to Trump has not always translated into greater influence over the administration’s agenda.
In just the past few months, members of Trump’s Cabinet and agency heads have regularly found themselves blindsided, overruled or scrambling to implement the president’s announcements on some of the most sensitive issues in their portfolios. The president countermanded Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the U.S. military posture in Europe, committing 5,000 troops after Hegseth canceled a deployment to Poland . (The Pentagon declined to comment.) Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Congress that while his department had been working on it, he was “ not ready to discuss ” how Treasury would implement Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 checks to Americans if Republicans won the election. The president reversed Mullin’s pause on Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle stops, with a post on Truth Social, while the White House withdrew Mullin’s pick to oversee the agency. (“President Trump and I are on the same page,” Mullin later wrote in a social media post .)
Many members of the Cabinet appear content with the exchange of power for proximity. Those who have thrived have accepted that they are not autonomous policymakers, but advisers whose views Trump may consider alongside those of many others — at times waiting silently for his social media posts to learn where he stands. And those who have been ousted — including the heads of the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security and Labor removed in rapid succession this spring — have learned that the ideological alignment and personal loyalty that earned them their jobs are not enough to survive in them.
“President Trump has assembled the most talented Cabinet in history who work every day to implement his commonsense agenda and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokesperson Liz Huston said in a written statement. To the suggestion that Trump’s appointees treat him like a monarch, spokesperson Davis Ingle said, “President Trump is working tirelessly on behalf of the American people to fulfill his commonsense America First agenda that nearly 80 million people elected him for.”
We attempted to speak with every member of Trump’s second-term Cabinet about what it is like to serve the president, and reached many of them. We ultimately interviewed more than three dozen people, including executive branch staffers and former officials, granting some anonymity to discuss those sensitive dynamics with full candor.
“During the first term, maybe like 20% of people thought Trump was saving the world, and like 80% of the people thought they were saving the world from Trump,” said a senior administration official. “Now it’s like 95% of people think Trump is saving the world, and so they’re believers.”
Linda McMahon was in her living room late one night, shortly after Trump won his second election, when her phone rang. Trump wanted to know if the woman who had led the Small Business Administration in his first term — and had been CEO of World Wrestling Entertainment before that — wanted to be his secretary of Education.
“Mr. President,” McMahon recalled telling him, “you know that I have not been in the world of education.”
“Well, you did graduate from college, didn’t you?” he responded, according to McMahon’s recollection.
Trump wasn’t looking for someone with education credentials. What he wanted instead was another business leader that would deliver a “return on investment” in the Department of Education. He also said her goal would be to put herself “out of a job” with the eventual downsizing of the department, she recalled.

articles.title_zh: Iran Still Awaits ‘Official’ U.S. Response Despite Trump’s Rebuff of Cease-Fire Offer
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s latest proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as experts say the United States president believes Washington has more to gain by waiting than by accepting Tehran’s terms at this moment.
“I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters on Saturday, arguing that Iran wants an agreement because it is “losing so badly”.
“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” Trump said. “I’d like to make a deal too. But that deal would not be acceptable.”
On Sunday, Iranian ⁠⁠Foreign ⁠⁠Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had ⁠⁠seen the initial reaction from ‌‌Trump to its proposal but had yet to receive a response through ⁠⁠mediators. In the latest diplomatic efforts, Qatar has played a role in mediating talks between Iran and the US on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York.
Iran’s seven-day proposal included Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales, releasing an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observing a wider regional ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran would then reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations with Washington on a final agreement.
The latest proposals are similar to the June memorandum of understanding (MoU) the two countries signed. But the MoU collapsed last month due to differences on the terms of the deal, which resulted in an escalation in attacks, particularly in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which essentially remains under Iranian blockade.
According to experts, Trump’s rejection suggested that while both sides continue to publicly leave the door open for diplomacy, they remain far apart over who should make the first concessions.
“Trump’s calculation looks fairly straightforward. He believes the combination of the naval blockade and economic isolation is finally squeezing Iran hard enough that Tehran’s latest proposal is evidence of weakness rather than an offer Washington needs to seize,” Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
His public argument that Iran is “losing badly” is important because it suggests he thinks time is improving the US bargaining position, Krieg said.
A key part of Trump’s calculation appears to be a belief that the economic pressure on Iran has not yet run its course.
The Trump administration has escalated economic pressure on Tehran, tightening its naval blockade while imposing sanctions targeting Iranian oil revenues and threatening secondary sanctions against countries doing business with Tehran.
Last week, the US imposed aviation sanctions on Iran, disrupting flights. This came weeks after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, promising to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.
Richard Weitz, a senior nonresident associate fellow at the NATO Defence College, told Al Jazeera that the White House may believe it can “wait a bit and get better terms”.
There is also concern in Washington about Iran’s proposed sequencing, he said.
Therefore, Weitz said Washington may be calculating that “economic pressure over time will induce the Iranian government to make more concessions”.
“This is what occurred arguably a decade ago, leading to the 2015 Iran nuclear deal as the Iranian government decided it [the US] needed to end the economic sanctions in return for making concessions on its nuclear programme,” he added.
It is, therefore, possible that “we could see the same kind of trade-off in the coming months”.
However, waiting for a deal also carries considerable political risk for the US president, experts said, because his Republican Party could lose November’s midterm elections.
A late August Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested 63 percent of Americans opposed the US-Israel war on Iran while 31 percent supported it. Rising fuel and transportation costs could also feed into broader cost-of-living concerns before the elections.
The problem for Trump is that time does not only increase pressure on Iran, Krieg said. “The gamble is that time cuts both ways,” he noted.
With the midterms approaching, Trump does not want to appear to lift the blockade, waive oil sanctions and release Iranian assets simply to regain access to a waterway that Iran itself disrupted, Krieg said.
“But every additional week also means elevated energy prices, continued military exposure and mounting pressure on Gulf partners.”
The essential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted oil and gas flows from the Gulf nations, which depend on energy exports to finance their budgets.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s proposal could be viewed as “kind of throwing a bone to Trump” by offering a potential route towards lower oil and gas prices before the vote.
However, Iran may decide “to make Trump pay for declining the proposal and the increased economic pressure the country is under”, he told Al Jazeera.
“They may decide that this is the time to escalate … just as the midterms are approaching.”
The Republican Party is not doing well in the polls, and a number of its candidates are “distancing themselves” from Trump, he noted. Polls indicated that Republicans could lose their slim majorities in the US Congress.
It’s not just the Iranians under severe economic pressure because of the US naval blockade and ongoing sanctions, “it’s also the Trump administration,” Elmasry said.
Trump “wants Tehran to reopen Hormuz without Washington paying the full economic and political price Iran is currently demanding”, Krieg said.
“The danger is that he is confusing Iranian pain with Iranian willingness to capitulate. Those are not the same thing.”
Iran is undoubtedly under pressure. Krieg said the sanctions and blockade are “biting”, which is precisely why Tehran needs an agreement.
But additional pressure does not necessarily produce additional concessions.
Iran could instead increase the costs of the conflict for its adversaries, Krieg said, including through the Strait of Hormuz, regional infrastructure and potentially Bab al-Mandeb, another strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa.
In recent weeks, the strategic weight of Bab al-Mandeb has increased dramatically after the Iran-aligned Houthis expanded their control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline.
This advance in effect has handed the Houthis unrestricted access to the narrow waterway, a worrying development for global shipping given the group’s track record of targeting vessels, including Israeli-linked ships, in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
The Houthis have already declared a naval blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea, which Riyadh began to use as an alternative shipping route to Hormuz for its oil exports.
“So this can backfire,” Krieg warned. “Trump thinks Iran’s clock is running faster than America’s. Tehran thinks the opposite: that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, global energy markets and ultimately Trump himself have a lower tolerance for prolonged disruption than Iran has for economic punishment.”
Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, similarly told Al Jazeera that Tehran may now be “less worried about overplaying their hand than they are underplaying their hand”.

“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian said.

articles.title_orig: Why The iPhone Duo Could Be Beneficial For Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8
articles.title_zh: Why The iPhone Duo Could Be Beneficial For Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8
articles.content_orig:
How Apple's entry into the foldable market could boost its biggest rival.
Apple recently unveiled the iPhone Duo , its first foldable phone. Although it won't hit stores until next month, the announcement alone was enough to get the smartphone world talking. And while Apple is making its first attempt at the format, others, like Samsung, have been doing this for some time — the original 2019 Galaxy Fold was one of the first mainstream foldable devices.
As it turns out, the iPhone Duo announcement might also end up being a positive for competing devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 . It's not as if Samsung is celebrating the Duo, but the hype surrounding it ends up drawing more attention to the foldable category overall.
Samsung currently leads the foldable device segment, but that market slice doesn't even come close to conventional smartphones. IDC estimates that about 20.6 million foldable phones were shipped last year, but that's only a fraction of the overall smartphone market. Global smartphone shipments reached 1.25 billion last year, giving an idea of just how niche the foldable phone market still is. But the iPhone Duo has the potential to change that, and we're already seeing the first effects.
Recent reports suggest that more people are buying the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 following the announcement of the iPhone Duo. It's possible that people are finally starting to pay attention to foldables, or maybe enthusiasts want to give the form factor a try before the iPhone Duo goes on sale. Either way, Samsung is well aware of this, and has already dropped the price of its foldable phones in some markets. This is just one of many examples of how competition ultimately benefits consumers.
With Apple now in the race, other players will have to step up their game to compete. The result will be more available options and likely broader price ranges, too. There's only one iPhone Duo for now, but Samsung, for example, already has a variety of foldables available. These range from the relatively affordable Galaxy Z Flip7 FE to the chic and expensive Z Fold 8 Ultra . Eventually, the competition might even push Apple to make a cheaper iPhone Duo model.
There's a benefit on the hardware and software side, too. Although foldable phones aren't breaking news anymore, Apple has shown how it always finds a way to catch up. For instance, the company hasn't completely solved the screen crease issue, but it looks significantly less noticeable on the iPhone Duo thanks to a matte nano-textured layer. There's little doubt that other folding phone makers will follow suit soon.
The same goes for the new user interface designed specifically for the iPhone Duo . It's still iOS, but clearly designed for a device that can be used in multiple layouts — folded, unfolded or half-open. Many current foldable devices simply stretch or shrink the same interface across all screens, which ends up looking unfinished. Also, there are already developers porting the iPhone Duo's opening and closing animation to Android. It's not hard to imagine this becoming an industry standard before long.
So yes, Apple wasn't the first to make a foldable phone, and you may not even want to buy one. But this entry will likely end up shaping the entire foldable market anyway.

The White House has launched another taxpayer-funded television ad before the midterms, this time featuring imagery of President Donald Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad , echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.
The ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game.
The Trump administration has drawn widespread attention for its airing of ads featuring the president just over a month before the November midterms. The White House has compared the ads to previous administrations running public service announcements about Medicare, Obamacare and promoting Covid-19 vaccination, saying in a statement that its new commercials “are very clearly not campaign ads.”
The latest ad appears nearly identical to the majority of a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign. The video on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text, while “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the White House-funded ad.
This is the third government-funded ad to be captured in recent days by the media tracker AdImpact. An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism, with text on the screen that touts his administration’s accomplishments, such as “reigniting American manufacturing.”
A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”
The White House declined to elaborate on how the first ad was being funded but defended it as part of “public service announcements” to promote national pride.
“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”
That ad drew scrutiny from the government watchdog group Common Cause, which suggested it could violate rules against using taxpayer dollars for “propaganda.”
“I don’t think you have to be a legal scholar and wonder why the president has to use taxpayer funds to promote his image” this close to an election, Carol Evans, the vice president for policy at Common Cause, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: French clergy abuse survivors praise meeting with Pope Leo XIV, say he listened, was informed
articles.title_zh: French clergy abuse survivors praise meeting with Pope Leo XIV, say he listened, was informed
articles.content_orig:
Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting with survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit to France .
Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday, Pope Leo XIV called on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.
“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.
Leo privately met seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.
Afterwards, the survivors said the pope had listened to them, was informed of their cases and said more work was needed to respond to the scandal.
Five of the seven survivors who met Leo held a press conference in Lourdes, the Catholic shrine that has long drawn sick and disabled people and more recently victims of abuse.
Jean-Marie Delbos said he never thought the day would come when he would meet a pope. He asked Leo to bless a photo of his grandmother, which he did. “It was extraordinary,” he said.
During a homily to the faithful, the pope also attacked medically assisted dying as immoral “false compassion”, in a staunch articulation of the Catholic church’s teaching that all human life must be defended from conception until natural death.
After years of debate, France formally adopted legislation last month allowing incurably ill adults the right to “aid in dying” , joining a small number of countries with similar laws, including Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Canada.
The pope said: “It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral.”
The pope was due to take part in six events while in Lourdes, including a meeting with staff and patients at the shrine’s care centre.
Lourdes has drawn millions of sick and disabled believers seeking a cure from its spring waters since the Catholic church officially recognised visions of the Virgin Mary reported by a local girl in 1858. Arriving there in a white popemobile on Saturday night, however, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing more than two dozen women over three decades.
Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.
Rupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.
Among the survivors who will meet the pope is a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, whose former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to be the biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.

In an interview published last year, the pope spoke of the “crisis” of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.
The first official papal visit to France in 18 years follows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.
France’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation after a landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.
On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.
“You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération .
The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.
The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).

articles.content_orig:
SALT LAKE CITY — Record high diesel prices are hitting Utah truckers hard, and have some of them concerned that they'll have to get out of the trucking business.
On Thursday, the cost of a gallon of diesel fuel in Utah reached $6.60 per gallon, the highest it's ever been in Utah according to AAA.
Just a year ago, AAA said the cost to put a gallon of diesel in your vehicle was $3.73.
The cost for diesel fuel has increased mostly because of the ongoing U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, which has impacted how tankers maneuver through the Strait of Hormuz. And Russia reports that recent attacks on its refining infrastructure have impacted its oil exports.
Jamal Goldsmith owns a trucking company in Utah, and said that if prices continue at this rate he may be forced to shut down.
He said other small trucking companies are in the same boat.
"I was just talking to a random driver at a rest area," Goldsmith told KSL. "He was telling me that he doesn't think he'll keep going much longer. Because, we're not making any headway. Whatever we're making is going back to the truck, to pay for the fuel, to pay for all the expenses. After all that's said and done, there's very little for you."
Goldsmith said he will most likely make a decision on his company by the end of November.

articles.title_orig: 'Avengers: Endgame Encore' Scores Massive $86 Million Globally
articles.title_zh: 'Avengers: Endgame Encore' Scores Massive $86 Million Globally
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
“ Avengers: Endgame ” returned to theaters and assembled a massive $86 million globally, including $26 million in North America and $60 million overseas.
Disney and Marvel’s 2019 blockbuster was already the second-highest-grossing movie in box office history with $2.79 billion; this weekend’s haul brings the movie’s staggering tally to $2.88 billion. It’s only $39 million behind 2009’s “Avatar,” which is the biggest worldwide release of all time with $2.9 billion.
Disney and Marvel reissued “Avengers: Endgame” to stoke excitement for “ Avengers: Doomsday ,” which opens in December. The upcoming comic book tentpole, which reunites just about every superhero on this planet (and others) and reintroduces Robert Downey Jr. not as Iron Man but as the villain Doctor Doom, is expected to be one of the biggest movies of the year. This re-release offered new footage as well as a chance to introduce viewers to the studio’s new take on premium large formats called “Infinity Vision.” It’s not a new technology but rather a “certification” that guarantees movie theaters will “meet rigorous technical standards,” per Disney. (As a note, “Avengers: Doomsday” won’t have access to Imax, the most ubiquitous of the PLFs, because “Dune: Part III” debuts on the same day and has the entire Imax footprint exclusively for three weeks.)
“Bringing ‘Avengers: Endgame’ back to theaters with an exclusive look at ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ is a smart way to give audiences a reason to revisit the film on the big screen and build excitement for what comes next,” says Rentrack’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “‘Avengers: Doomsday’ is poised for one of the biggest opening weekend performances of all time.”
Directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, “Avengers: Doomsday” will be the 39th installment in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. It’s the most successful film franchise in history with $35.07 billion across all movies, a benchmark that was recently lifted by this summer’s juggernaut “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” with $2.2 billion.
“Avengers: Endgame Encore,” which the re-release has been dubbed, beat out several new releases to top domestic and global box office charts. Including this weekend’s grosses, “Endgame” strengthened its position as the third-largest North American release of all time with $884 million. Meanwhile, in a new milestone, “Avengers: Endgame” became the second movie ever to clear $2 billion at the international box office.
In terms of new releases, Paramount’s wilderness thriller “The Heart of the Beast” opened to $30.1 million from 63 markets. Along with a softer $20 million start in North America, the film has collected $50.1 million globally. Since it carries a hefty $82 million budget, “Heart of the Beast” will rely on staying power and interest at the international box office to recoup in its theatrical run. Reviews and word-of-mouth should help; “The Heart of the Beast” landed a strong 87% on Rotten Tomatoes and “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. David Ayer (“The Beekeeper”) directed “Heart of Beast,” which stars Pitt as a retired veteran who navigates a brutal 58-mile trek to safety after he and his trusted combat dog survive a harrowing plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness.
Another newcomer, Universal and DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island,” struggled with $7.8 million from 34 markets. The movie has yet to land in several key international territories. Globally, “Forgotten Island” has earned just $20.6 million, including a softer-than-expected $12.8 million domestically. Universal shelled out $80 million to produce the family film, so the studio needs the positive reviews and audience reception to help “Forgotten Island” stick around beyond its debut. Directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, the story follows around two best friends who get stranded in a mystical world. H.E.R., Dave Franco and Jenny Slate lead the voice cast.
Earlier this week, Universal became the first to cross $5 billion worldwide in 2026, fueled by Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” with $1.75 billion and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” with $1 billion.

The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sept. 27, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Republican Louisiana Senator John Kennedy. Good morning to you, Senator. Senator, the president seems to be dangling some interest in diplomacy. The U.S. president also seems to be somewhat interested, but the Wall Street Journal is also reporting President Trump has a secret plan to restart the bombing campaign in Iran after the midterm elections. That's 37 days from now. Is that renewed bombing something you support?
SEN. JOHN KENNEDY: Well, I don't know. I haven't seen the classified intelligence. Iran- Iran made an offer recently to the president. It was not a serious offer. The president's not Bambi's baby brother. He turned it down. We need to continue doing what we're doing. The sanctions, the blockade. The truth is, if you- if you're fair minded at all, Iran is a sucking chest wound and the world is safer for it. It's public and private sector is held together with duct tape and spit. Now, there's- there's just one problem. The strait is at least partially closed, and it's affected the price of oil and oil's in everything, including gasoline. And- and it's painful as- as hell. And we've got to either figure out a way to- to settle this thing, to get the strait open or to escalate. I would not send in troops. We could send in troops and we could open the strait. But once you send them in, you've got to leave them there. And that creates a whole new host of problems.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, and the broader question of to what end, since the president has said, you know, Iran is about to capitulate any day now. But when we look at the politics of this out in Iowa and Michigan, we've seen Republican candidates who are going to be on the ballot in November, call for an end to the Iran war. In the Senate, we've seen 14 votes to date, objecting to it- two passed. I mean, I know those are symbolic, but this is reflective of frustration within your own party here. Should the president be more aware of public opinion?
SEN. KENNEDY: Well, look, here's- none of this is advanced calculus. Here's- I've- I've- I've been to just about every battleground state helping my mates. Here's what I've learned. When- when moms and dads lie down to sleep at night and can't, they're not lying there worried about whether the football coaches are happy or whether the press is biased or the other things that we've been talking about. They're worried about the cost of living.
SEN. KENNEDY: And- and they're a little worried about Iran because they don't understand why, but they know the two are inextricably linked. And we've got to be straight up and address those things. Here's my prediction for the midterms, Margaret. The experts will be wrong. They almost always are. Not- not- none of these guys have ever run a campaign in their natural lives. It's going to be close. It would help if the president would stay focused on cost of living. And I would like to see him give a nationwide address.
SEN. KENNEDY: Or let Rubio and General Caine do it and explain why we went into Iran, why we're winning, and how we're going to get out.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. You've been making that recommendation for some time. You did it last time you were with us over the summer. The White House has not to date, but--
SEN. KENNEDY: Well- well- well, the- the- the president doesn't take orders from me. He barely takes suggestions. But I'm pretty persistent, and I'm going to keep recommending it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about something else the executive branch just did without Congress. On Friday, the White House informed Congressional leaders that he, the president, unilaterally canceled nearly $1 billion in Congressionally approved funds and did it without Congress's consent. You sit on Appropriations. The chair of that committee, Susan Collins, said this was the latest attempt to undermine Congress's constitutional power of the purse, and that this is a clear violation of the law. She wants to take action against these illegal actions. Do you share her concern? Are you going to join her effort?
SEN. KENNEDY: I love- I love Susan like a taco, but she's wrong. First, Congress didn't approve this stuff. When Congress appropriates money, we do it in broad care- categories. For example, I'm making this up- $250 million to improve relations with sub-Sahara Africa. And then the money goes to the bureaucracy. And a lot of times the bureaucracy wastes it. Spending porn is what I call it. That's how we ended up with millions of dollars for circumcisions in- in Zambia and electric buses in Rwanda.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you're okay with this?
SEN. KENNEDY: What- what the president- yeah, I'm fine with it. What- what- if you read what- what Russ Vought wants to actually cut, what he wants- what he wants to cut is aid to NGOs who support illegal immigration. And he also wants to cut some money that the bureaucracy has decided to give to help pay down, not our debt, but foreign debt. This stuff- spending porn. Congress didn't approve it. Now Susan is worried about them doing this to the NIH grants. I don't think they ought to do it to the NIH grants, but this is spending porn that they're cutting--
SEN. KENNEDY: --and Congress ought to be- Congress ought to get up off its ice-cold, lazy butt and cut it itself. But since we're not--
SEN. KENNEDY: --I'm glad- I'm glad that Russ Vought's doing it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're talking about concern about wasteful spending.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You were very sharp in your questioning of then-Secretary Kristi Noem in regard to some ads that DHS had been running, using taxpayer money to bolster her public image. Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program. It's on all major networks, it's on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there's a voice praising him as, quote, "the toughest, most resilient person I ever met." And at the end, it says "paid for by the U.S. government." Is that the best use of taxpayer money?
SEN. KENNEDY: Well, first, as to Secretary Noem, what she did was master class dumb. she spent $220 million on commercials about her, and I called her out on it. Number two--
MARGARET BRENNAN: This looks like a commercial about President Trump.

articles.title_orig: UK's Burnham pledges to fight next election on social care reform
articles.title_zh: UK's Burnham pledges to fight next election on social care reform
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.
The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.
Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.
Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month .
While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded.
Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.
Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.
In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.
Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work.
"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."
Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.
Burnham said the changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".
But he said that "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" in terms of how the proposals would be funded.
When he was told it had been estimated that a system for everyone in England that is free at the point of use could cost taxpayers £18bn a year, Burnham replied: "It's not that high."
He said people already face a "huge cost" at the moment and that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out".
Burnham added there is also a cost to the NHS due to the "huge number" of people in hospitals across England who cannot be discharged home "because the social care isn't there".
Asked whether everyone will have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham replied: "It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS."
He said the details developed by Baroness Casey would be subject to cross-party talks in a bid to "build consensus".
Baroness Casey was originally tasked by former PM Sir Keir Starmer to deliver her review of social care in 2028, but Burnham asked her to bring that forward to next summer.
On the timeline, Burnham added: "I'm going to say that we stick to the manifesto because I have to keep people's trust, and there are commitments in the manifesto that would make it hard to do in this Parliament."
The Labour manifesto in 2024 made clear commitments on tax, including not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT.
Burnham added: "I don't think you can reform this system without consensus. I will develop a very clear plan and I will put that plan to the public at a general election and that will be where the plan gets tested and people will then be able to decide."
Philp said tax increases would be a "red line" for the Conservatives and they would "not under any circumstances" support more of them.
He said the country is "already taxed too highly", telling the BBC: "If more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence we would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget."
Labour MP Darren Jones, who served as a cabinet minister in Sir Keir's government, said Burnham was being "very bold and brave" on social care.
He said: "Politics is about prioritisation and these things do cost money and so we'll need to see the detail of that policy."
He told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms.
The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said Burnham can show he is "serious about fixing care" by getting on with the cross-party talks that began in July.
He added: "This can't just be a series of No 10 headlines with no real action."
Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Andy Burnham refuses to rule out his universal death tax.
"He's too weak to cut the benefits bill so he's coming for your home instead."
Burnham accused previous generations of politicians of "cowardice" for failing to reform social care, although his push for change is not without jeopardy.
He previously produced a plan for a national care service while serving as health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government.
It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution, including from people's estates after they had died.
The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election.
At the 2017 general election, then-Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May was accused of trying to introduce a "dementia tax" by proposing that people receiving care at home pay for the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000.
The policy sparked a political outcry and the Conservatives lost their majority in the House of Commons at the election.

articles.title_orig: Some Republicans Issue a New Call on Trump’s War With Iran: End It Now
articles.title_zh: Some Republicans Issue a New Call on Trump’s War With Iran: End It Now
articles.content_orig:
This article was featured in the Daily Prospect newsletter. Sign up for it here.
After a notable absence, an anti-war movement has emerged to finally challenge a president over the unpopular conflict in Iran. Not in the streets so much, but in ads and statements from Republicans trying to salvage their doomed election campaigns.
“The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly,” said Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers in a digital ad. Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH) made almost the same verbatim statement to Politico, suggesting some coordination among this new iteration of the National Mobilization Committee. Even Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chair currently being left for dead in North Carolina’s Senate race against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, tentatively conceded that farmers were being hurt from the conflict due to fuel and fertilizer prices.
“I just believe we should be exiting Iran, that it’s time to move on,” agreed Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany, who incidentally wasn’t present for a vote to end the war when he had an opportunity last week. Two of Tiffany’s Republican colleagues in the neighboring state of Iowa, Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, did vote for the war powers resolution to end the war, making a total of seven Republicans helping to pass that resolution through the House. Rep. Ashley Hinson, running for Senate in Iowa, said Monday that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” despite voting against that war powers resolution just days earlier, the sixth time she has done so this year. The Senate version of that war powers vote, held on Thursday, failed, with Husted and all other Republicans fretting about re-election (except Susan Collins, who has voted for war powers resolutions before) voting against stopping the war.
The key here is that on everything that matters, Trump and Republicans in Congress are fully aligned.
The national media loves itself some good intraparty conflict. Stories about the Republican “fever breaking,” egged on by Democratic leaders, have been a perennial since before Donald Trump descended the golden escalator. Now, with less than 40 days to an election that is shaping up to be an epochal disaster for the GOP, that long-anticipated distancing from the most unpopular president headed into a midterm since Harry Truman in 1946 is upon us. Not just the war, but a growing number of Trump’s policies are being condemned, debated, and rejected, at rapid speed.
As a policy and even a political matter, this shift is almost 700 days late and about $3 trillion short . For 99.9 percent of the past two years, Republicans have fallen in line with every insane maneuver and utterance from this administration; at best, they would pretend not to have heard them. Only when accountability from the voters is imminent have we seen the emergence of “independent” thought and behavior—that is, evasive action induced solely by panicked self-interest, like an amoeba shrinking away from a sharp object.
To be heartened by the courage of Paul LePage, running in a Trump +9 seat in northern Maine that was recently shifted to a toss-up by none other than Fox News , for speaking out that his son-in-law’s father is “being deported because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington,” you would have to ignore LePage’s long history of anti-immigrant and racist remarks and his ad released just this week proudly touting his record facilitating deportation as governor. To raise a fist in solidarity with Maria Elvira Salazar, in a +15 Trump seat, running an ad about Trump’s deportation policies going too far, you would have to forget her vote to set up and fund the current mass deportation architecture. So did Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, who recently castigated ICE for not working with local law enforcement in the state.
The fact that Husted and Hinson and others wouldn’t vote their own convictions on the Iran war shows how performative and inauthentic this distance is. Trump knows this, which is why you haven’t heard much from him about it. If anything, in fact, his own administration is following the fair-weather detractors, swinging frantically at changes that they hope will make voters forget the last two years.
The Domestic Policy Council is trying to cut Trump’s foreign beef imports , which ranchers have savaged as destructive of their livelihoods and misaligned to bring down retail prices. But the White House denied that anything would change. The Senate is likely to stay in session next week to try to save Sen. Husted’s job with a roll call vote on a bill he co-authored, the Ratepayer Protection Act. This would mirror the White House’s voluntary pledge by utilities that data center development will not raise the cost of power bills. But Trump’s positive outlook on data centers, which is wildly out of step with public opinion, clearly hasn’t changed given the siting of new facilities on public lands . Adding to a voluntary pledge with legislation that is also mostly voluntary—it sets a framework for states to force data center developers to pay for utility upgrades, without requiring that states apply those rules—won’t erase this position.
The most farcical example of save-the-majority-based policymaking is how to handle the record high cost of diesel fuel , a function of both the Iran debacle and Ukrainian pulverizing of Russian refining infrastructure. The easiest way to ease energy spikes stemming from war would be to, you know, end the wars, but instead Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK), threatened with the loss of his seat, demanded an executive order to temporarily ban diesel exports. Trump lunged at this and a 90-day ban is in process , even as Trump’s own energy secretary said it wouldn’t work . The problem is that diesel is largely refined on the Gulf Coast, and there is no easy way to move it domestically elsewhere in the nation. It follows that higher global prices (which an export ban would perpetuate) would increase costs within parts of the U.S. that get imported diesel. Plus, refiners are not guaranteed to pass through savings that come with higher domestic supply, and storage needs would likely slow down gas refining and shift the price spike toward that product.
The key here is that on everything that matters—war and peace, the actual implementation of deportation policy, even absurd things like the diesel export ban—Trump and Republicans in Congress are fully aligned. Anything above a meek plea that they feel the pain they inflicted on voters, or would do anything whatsoever about it the second the election is over, is not in evidence.
Since January 20, 2025, the Republican Congress could have stopped the imposition of tariffs through existing mechanisms. They could have cut off funding for wars they don’t like. They could have tied continued defiance of appropriations laws they passed by cutting the personal presidential travel budget. They could have impeached and removed him from office, with Democratic support. Instead they support Trump’s every whim in almost perfect lockstep, no matter how crazy. These deathbed conversions are preposterous, and everybody knows it.
One final thought: I understand why congressional Republicans are worried about losing their fancy offices and the pretend trappings of a power they chose not to wield. I’m less sure why Trump cares. Sure, in theory, a Democratic Congress could take up the countermeasures Republicans refused to enact and halt Trump’s expansive agenda. But given what we’ve just seen on the Paramount merger , it’s a real stretch to think that Democrats have the will or fortitude or even interest in doing that. So what’s Trump so concerned about?
David Dayen is the executive editor of The American Prospect. He is the author of Monopolized: Life in the Age of Corporate Power and Chain of Title: How Three Ordinary Americans Uncovered Wall Street’s Great Foreclosure Fraud.

There are a lot of $300-$400 headphones on the market right now, and most of them blur together. I spent the last few weeks with the Sennheiser Momentum 5 to determine if this pair actually stands out, testing everything from sound quality and noise cancellation to comfort and battery life.
At $399.99, the Momentum 5 sit right in the middle of the premium headphone market. That puts them up against the pricier Sony WH-1000XM6 and Apple AirPods Max 2, while offering a more affordable option for anyone looking for high-end headphones.
Starting with sound, vocals sound natural and the bass is strong without taking over. The headphones allow you to start noticing little things in music, like a background harmony or a guitar string that cheaper headphones often tend to miss. If I had to describe the sound in one word, it’d be balanced.
The headphones support Dolby Atmos, which essentially means that music or movies sound like they’re coming from all around you instead of just left and right.
With this generation, Sennheiser doubled the microphone count to eight to improve the active noise cancellation (ANC). Voices and nearby chatter, which are usually the kind of sounds that can cut through weaker ANC, are noticeably quieter. Sennheiser claims this pair is up to three times more effective than the previous generation at blocking this type of noise.
Of course, it’s not quite at the level of blocking out everything like a plane’s engine, but it does the job effectively without making your ears feel weirdly pressurized as can be the case with some ANC headphones.
As for comfort, the headphones aren’t as premium-feeling as Apple or Sony headphones that I’ve tried in the past, but given that the Momentum 5 cost less than its competitors, it’s a trade-off that’s hard to complain about.
The battery life is genuinely impressive. It’s rated for up to 57 hours, and that figure held up in my testing. For context, that’s roughly twice the battery life of the Sony WH-1000XM6 and nearly three times that of the AirPods Max 2.
And when the battery does run out, a 10-minute charge gets you up to seven hours of playback, while a full charge takes about two hours.
A notable difference that the Momentum 5 offers that its competitors don’t is a user-replaceable cell, which means you can swap out the battery once it degrades instead of having to buy a whole new pair.
What I wasn’t expecting, but found surprisingly useful, was how thin the carrying case is. I’ve never really been able to fit a pair of headphones into my medium-sized purses, but the Momentum 5 fit perfectly. It’s also a big plus when traveling, since the case doesn’t take up much space in your luggage.
With the headphones’ companion app, Smart Control Plus, you can adjust a bunch of different settings. There’s an 8-band EQ that lets you tune the sound yourself or choose from one of Sennheiser’s presets. The app also lets you adjust the level of ANC rather than just switching it on or off, and there’s an anti-wind mode you can access there too. The “Sound Personalization” feature walks you through a listening test and creates a sound profile tailored to your hearing preferences.
The app gives you a decent amount of control over the Momentum 5, and I found it pretty easy to navigate as most of the settings are quite straightforward.
Overall, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 is a solid option at this price. They offer great sound, the battery life is excellent, and the downsides are pretty minor. They’re heavier than the Sony WH-1000XM6, and aren’t as comfortable as some Sony or Apple options, but at $399.99, they’re cheaper than both while still delivering where it matters.
